<reason>Both sides argued at a high level, but B exposed and repeatedly pressed a structural flaw in A's central "product/transaction vs. inferred profile" test: A's own worst-case villain (the desperate midnight shopper facing few sellers) is priced on time-of-purchase and local competition, i.e., transaction features that A's own rule would permit. B raised this in [B2.3] and again in [B4.7], and A never directly answered it, instead quietly shifting the operative line from "product vs. profile" to "disclosed vs. undisclosed" — a shift B had already flagged in [B2.5] and exploited. B also offered a more original and consistently developed causal story (uniform price as the price the affluent would pay, personalization as a discount mechanism off a ceiling price) that survived into the closing, and answered both pressure questions with direct A1/A2 responses that clarified rather than dodged the tension between narrow bans and broad disclosure mandates. A's closing point about algorithmic pricing defeating the "marginal shopper" discipline mechanism was the strongest moment of PRO's case, but B's final rejoinder (the same targeting mechanism underlies discounts, not just surcharges) left that clash live rather than resolved in A's favor. On balance, B did more of the decisive comparative work and left fewer of its own claims exposed.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's repeated point ([B2.3], reiterated unanswered in [B4.7]) that A's own "product vs. profile" line actually permits A's chosen villain case (the desperate late-night shopper), which A never squarely answered across two further speeches.</best_rebuttal>
